briefs.title: Tax Fight Becomes a Campaign Issue as Operators Adapt — While DC Buys the Industry More Runway
briefs.top: In Michigan, the 24% wholesale tax is now a bona fide 2026 governor's-race issue with candidates from both parties pledging relief, even as savvy operators like Rize find ways to share the burden and keep growing. Nationally, momentum keeps building — Congress just bought the hemp industry another month, federal psychedelic vouchers are compressing FDA review timelines, and rescheduling proceedings are heading toward closing arguments.
briefs.label: Morning Brief

local.text: Rize, which runs three Upper Michigan locations, is sustaining growth despite the wholesale tax by negotiating cost-sharing arrangements with suppliers — splitting the burden instead of eating it alone, a playbook other operators are starting to copy.

Jars Cannabis notched a regulatory win in Madison Heights, securing removal of a Flock surveillance camera targeting the dispensary — a rare enforcement rollback that operators statewide are watching closely.

Fields Cannary is pushing the retail format further than almost any Michigan operator has gone: the Muskegon development is targeting a fall opening for its dispensary, with a full-service restaurant to follow — a hospitality-forward bet on cannabis tourism even in a tight-margin year.

Tax relief is now a real campaign plank: GOP nominee John James is proposing to cut Michigan's cannabis excise tax from 10% to 5% as part of his 'Freedom Agenda,' while Democratic hopeful Chris Swanson has already pledged to repeal the 24% wholesale tax — giving operators leverage heading into November regardless of who wins.

The hard number: Higher Love closed five of its nine U.P. locations, blaming the tax directly, and statewide active retail licenses slipped from 845 to 836 over the past year — but a fresh House repeal bill (HB 6224) is now on the table, giving the contraction a legislative off-ramp.

national.text: The FDA handed psychedelics its biggest boost in decades: Commissioner's National Priority Vouchers now let Compass Pathways (psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression), Usona Institute (psilocybin for MDD) and Transcend Therapeutics (methylone for PTSD) compress FDA review from roughly ten months down to just one to two months.

Federal marijuana rescheduling hit the closing-argument stage in late August, with the DEA hearing process moving toward a Schedule III determination — a real procedural milestone even as advocates caution a filing isn't a rule change yet.

President Trump signed the spending bill delaying the federal hemp THC ban, pushing most new restrictions from November 12 to December 11 — buying the hemp industry another month to lobby for a regulatory framework instead of outright prohibition.

M&A is heating up on rescheduling optimism: Vireo Growth's acquisition spree, including the former 'Uber of Weed' delivery platform, is being read by investors as a signal of confidence following Trump's executive order reclassifying cannabis to a less dangerous drug.

Rescheduling protections are getting real paperwork behind them: the DEA is now sending Colorado medical cannabis businesses a detailed 26-question compliance list to qualify for federal protections tied to the Schedule III move — bureaucratic, but a concrete sign the policy is moving from theory to implementation.
